SYNTHETIC TEST MATERIAL

US HISTORY (11th Grade) - Fall 2026
Instructor: Ms. Danielle Okafor-Reyes, Room 214, Lincoln Ridge High School (fictional)
Office hours: Tuesdays and Thursdays, 7:15-7:45 AM, or by appointment
Textbook: The American Story, 4th ed. (class set) plus weekly primary-source packets

COURSE DESCRIPTION
This course surveys US history from colonial settlement through Reconstruction and the Gilded Age. Students practice analyzing primary sources, writing document-based arguments, and connecting causes to effects.

WEEKLY SCHEDULE (week of)
Wk 1 - Aug 31: Course intro; Native America and European contact
Wk 2 - Sep 7 (no school Mon, Labor Day): Colonial settlement; Jamestown and New England
Wk 3 - Sep 14: Colonial economy, slavery, and the Atlantic world
Wk 4 - Sep 21: Road to Revolution; Declaration of Independence
Wk 5 - Sep 28: The Revolutionary War; Articles of Confederation
Wk 6 - Oct 5: Constitutional Convention; Federalists vs. Anti-Federalists; Bill of Rights
Wk 7 - Oct 12: Washington, Hamilton, Jefferson; first political parties
Wk 8 - Oct 19: Louisiana Purchase, Marbury v. Madison, War of 1812
Wk 9 - Oct 26: Market Revolution; Missouri Compromise; Jacksonian Democracy
Wk 10 - Nov 2: Unit review; MIDTERM UNIT TEST Thursday Nov 5
Wk 11 - Nov 9: Reform movements; Manifest Destiny
Wk 12 - Nov 16: Slavery and sectionalism; Compromise of 1850; Kansas-Nebraska
Wk 13 - Nov 23 (no school Thu-Fri, Thanksgiving): Election of 1860 and secession
Wk 14 - Nov 30: The Civil War
Wk 15 - Dec 7: Reconstruction; the Gilded Age begins
Wk 16 - Dec 14: Review; FINAL EXAM Thursday Dec 17

QUIZ AND EXAM DATES
Quiz 1 - Fri Sep 11: Colonial America (settlement, economy)
Quiz 2 - Fri Sep 25: American Revolution (causes, key documents)
Quiz 3 - Fri Oct 9: Constitution and Bill of Rights
Quiz 4 - Fri Oct 23: Early Republic, 1800-1824 (Louisiana Purchase, Marbury v. Madison, War of 1812, Missouri Compromise)
Midterm Unit Test - Thu Nov 5: Colonial era through Jacksonian Democracy
Quiz 5 - Fri Nov 13: Reform movements and Manifest Destiny
Quiz 6 - Fri Dec 4: Civil War and Reconstruction
Final Exam - Thu Dec 17: Cumulative, with emphasis on Units 3-4

GRADING BREAKDOWN
Quizzes (6, lowest dropped): 20%
Midterm Unit Test: 15%
Final Exam: 20%
Document-Based Essays (2): 15%
Homework and primary-source packets: 10%
Class participation and notebook checks: 10%
Grades: A 90-100, B 80-89, C 70-79, D 60-69, F below 60.

POLICIES
1. Late work: Homework loses 10% per day late, up to 3 days. After that it earns no more than 50%. Essays lose 5% per day. Ask before the due date if you need an extension.
2. Make-up quizzes and tests: If you are absent on a quiz or test day, you must schedule a make-up within 5 school days of your return. Pre-excused absences should be arranged in advance.
3. Academic honesty: All submitted work must be your own. Copying, sharing quiz answers, or using AI tools to write essays without permission results in a zero and a parent call. Cite all sources in the packets.

NOTE: The instructor may adjust dates for assemblies, weather, or pacing. Changes will be announced in class and posted on the class page.
notes:
US HIST NOTES - Jordan

TOPIC 1: Louisiana Purchase (1803)
- Jefferson (Dem-Rep) buys LA terr. from France, $15 mil. Napoleon needed $ for wars + lost Haiti (Saint-Domingue) after slave revolt
- ~828,000 sq mi, doubled size of US. approx 3 cents/acre (Ms. O said ~4 cents? check)
- Prob: Const. doesn't say prez can buy land!! Jefferson = strict constructionist but did it anyway. Used treaty power + "too good a deal" argument
- Key ppl: Robert Livingston, James Monroe (negotiators), Napoleon, Toussaint Louverture (indirectly)
- Lewis & Clark expedition 1804-06, w/ Sacagawea. Goal = map, find river route, meet tribes, science
- NOLA + Mississippi River = huge for western farmers (trade/ports)
- Effects: more land -> debate abt slavery in new states (leads to Missouri Compromise later)

TOPIC 2: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
- Background: Adams = Federalist, lost 1800 election. Appointed "midnight judges" b4 leaving office (Judiciary Act of 1801)
- William Marbury = one of them, commission not delivered. Madison (Sec of State under Jefferson) wouldn't deliver it
- Marbury sued, asked SC for writ of mandamus
- Chief Justice John Marshall (Federalist) -> ruled Marbury had a right to commission BUT Judiciary Act of 1789 section giving SC that power = unconstitutional
- RESULT = JUDICIAL REVIEW. SC can strike down laws that violate Const.
- Genius move: Marshall gave up small power to gain huge one. Jefferson's side "won" the case but Court won long-term
- Remember: Art. III, checks + balances

QUIZ 4 STUFF TO STUDY
- dates: 1803, 1804, 1812-1815, 1820
- Hartford Convention (Federalists vs war) -> Federalists decline
- Treaty of Ghent 1814 = basically status quo
- Battle of New Orleans (Jan 1815) AFTER treaty signed, Andrew Jackson hero
- Era of Good Feelings = Monroe

Chapter 9 - The Mlssouri Compromise (1820)

Background: By 1819 the Union had 11 free states and 11 slave states, so the balance in the Senate was eqaul. When Missouri asked to join as a slave state, Northerners feared the South would gain power in Congress.

Rep. James Tallmadge proposed banning further slavery in Missouri. The House passed it; the Senate rejccted it.

The Compromise: 
- Missouri enters as a slave state
- Maine enters as a free state (separated from Massachusetts)
- Slavery banned in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of lat. 36°30' [unreadable]

Henry Clay, the "Great Compromiser," helped pass the dea1 through Congress. Thomas Jefferson called the debate "a fire bell in the nlght." The compromise delayed conflict but did not setle the issue of slavery in the territories.
transcript:
Okay, um, so let's get started, everybody find a seat, please. Today we're talking about Jacksonian Democracy, so, uh, the 1820s and 1830s. And before we dive in, quick thing, I know a lot of you saw the game Friday, and, um, honestly I have never seen a halftime show with that many tubas, but anyway, let's get back to it.

So, um, think about the election of 1824. Andrew Jackson wins the most popular votes and the most electoral votes, but, uh, he doesn't have a majority. So who decides? The House of Representatives. And Henry Clay, who came in fourth, throws his support to John Quincy Adams. Adams wins. And then Adams names Clay as Secretary of State. Jackson's supporters call this the "corrupt bargain." Now, did a formal deal actually happen? Historians still argue about it, but the point is that Jackson's side was furious, and they spent the next four years organizing.

So in 1828, Jackson wins big. Um, and this is where the idea of the "common man" comes in. More white men could vote by then, because states were dropping property requirements. So the electorate gets much larger. Jackson presents himself as a man of the people, born in a log cabin more or less, a war hero from the Battle of New Orleans, and, you know, not one of the Eastern elites. His inauguration, so, there's this story that the crowd poured into the White House and, um, people stood on the furniture. Whether that's totally accurate or not, it shows how people saw it.

Now I want to be careful here. When we say democracy, we mean white male democracy. Women couldn't vote, enslaved people obviously couldn't, free Black men lost voting rights in several states during this period, and Native Americans were not citizens. So, um, keep that in mind. This will be on the exam, the idea that democracy expanded for some and shrank for others.

Okay, so the spoils system. Jackson fires a bunch of federal officials and replaces them with supporters. He says, basically, any ordinary person can do a government job. Critics said it was just rewarding loyalty. The phrase comes from, um, "to the victor belong the spoils."

Then we have the Bank War. Jackson hated the Second Bank of the United States. He thought it favored wealthy people and was too powerful and, uh, undemocratic. Congress passes a recharter in 1832, Jackson vetoes it. He wins re-election that year easily. Then he removes federal deposits and puts them into state banks, which critics called his "pet banks." Long term, that contributes to economic trouble, the Panic of 1837, which hits right after Van Buren takes office.

And then, um, the Indian Removal Act of 1830. This is the part that, honestly, is hard to talk about. Jackson pushes it through, the Cherokee fight it in court, Worcester v. Georgia, and the Supreme Court sides with the Cherokee, but, uh, Jackson basically ignores it. Then you get the Trail of Tears, 1838 to 1839, thousands of Cherokee die on the forced march west.

So what do I want you to take away? Jackson expanded political participation for many white men, but he also expanded executive power and, um, carried out policies that were devastating for Native peoples.

A couple of announcements. Quiz 4 originally Friday October 23 covers the Early Republic stuff, so Louisiana Purchase through the Missouri Compromise. Jackson will be on the midterm, which is Thursday November 5. Your document packet on the Cherokee is due Monday. Okay, so, um, open your books to chapter 10 and let's look at the cartoon of King Andrew the First.
